weaknesses: The main methodological contribution is limited in novelty: MF-NPE is essentially standard low-fidelity pretraining followed by full-network fine-tuning. There is no theoretical analysis, characterization of sample-complexity improvement, or principled criterion for when the low-fidelity model will help rather than cause negative transfer.

The baseline suite is inadequate for supporting the central claims. Most comparisons are only against NPE. In particular, MF-TSNPE is not compared with ordinary TSNPE, so its gains confound multifidelity initialization with the established benefit of sequential inference. There are also no competitive multifidelity-SBI methods, joint/multitask training alternatives, or controls using unrelated or deliberately degraded pretraining.

The efficiency analysis counts only high-fidelity simulations and does not normalize by total simulation and training cost. This is especially problematic for the neuron task, where the low-fidelity simulator is only about seven times cheaper: 100,000 low-fidelity simulations already cost roughly as much as 14,000 high-fidelity simulations, before neural-network training is counted. Consequently, the claimed one-to-two-order-of-magnitude computational saving is not established by wall-clock or cost-matched comparisons.

A-MF-TSNPE knowingly mixes adaptively selected parameters into the proposal without importance weighting or another proposal correction. Its training objective therefore generally targets a posterior under the altered sampling distribution rather than the desired prior. The paper provides neither a bias analysis nor calibration evidence for this variant, and its small gain on one toy task is insufficient to justify the method.

Experimental uncertainty is understated. Training simulations are fixed and repetitions vary mainly network initialization, so the confidence intervals do not capture variability from drawing a small high-fidelity dataset—the dominant source of uncertainty at budgets such as 50 or 100. Sequential variants are evaluated only on the OU task, and there is no systematic study of fidelity mismatch, negative transfer, or sensitivity to pretraining and fine-tuning choices.

Important implementation details are missing, including optimizer, learning rate, batch size, exact early-stopping rule, split proportions, seeds, C2ST configuration, and reference-posterior sample counts. The manuscript provides no usable code link. It is also unclear whether the sequential x-axis reports total simulations or the per-round M in Algorithms 2–3, which would imply five times as many simulations overall.

Several inconsistencies further impair reproducibility: the neuron stimulus is described as a noisy 0.3 nA current in the main text but as a 0.55 mV current in the appendix; the spiking models are described once as having 12 versus 14 parameters but elsewhere as 12 versus 24; and Appendix Figure 10 calls 50 versus 1,000 simulations a two-order-of-magnitude reduction although it is a factor of 20.

The neuroscience results use synthetic simulator-generated observations rather than empirical data. For the 24-parameter spiking model, evaluation relies largely on two firing-rate summaries and a broad 1–50 Hz plausibility criterion, with no posterior calibration, quantitative posterior-predictive discrepancy, sample counts, or uncertainty for the table. This evidence is too limited for the broad real-world applicability claims.
